subtopics.title: Project Classification, Life-Cycle Phases & the Planning Process
subtopics.subtitle: What a project is, how projects are classified, life-cycle phases, WBS and planning steps

concepts.text: What a Project Is

PMI's PMBOK defines a project as a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. Temporary means it has a definite start and end; unique means the output is not identical to anything produced before, even if the methods are familiar. A project differs from operations, which are ongoing and repetitive (running a power station is operations; building it is a project). Engineering projects such as roads, hydropower plants, buildings and software systems all share these features.
Characteristics commonly listed for a project:
items: Definite objectives and a defined scope of work.
A fixed time frame with start and completion dates, and a limited budget.
Unique output, so uncertainty and risk are always present.
A life cycle of distinct phases, with resource use rising and then falling.
A temporary, often multidisciplinary team led by a project manager.
Stakeholders (owner, consultant, contractor, financier, community) with different interests.

concepts.text: Classification of Projects

rows: Community water tap vs national highway
Cement plant, bridge, school, irrigation, e-governance
Public, private, joint venture, public-private partnership
Government road, IPP hydropower, BOT toll road
New factory vs upgrading an old canal
Private hotel vs rural health post

concepts.text: Project Life-Cycle Phases
PMBOK process groups follow the sequence initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, and closure:
items: Initiation (conception): idea identification, pre-feasibility and feasibility studies, project charter, go / no-go decision.
Planning (definition and design): scope, WBS, schedule, cost estimate, resource, procurement, quality and risk plans; detailed design.
Execution (implementation): procurement, construction or development, and mobilisation of the team and contractors.
Monitoring and control: runs alongside execution, comparing actual progress with the baseline and taking corrective action.
Closure (termination): handover, final accounts, release of resources, completion report and lessons learned.

concepts.text: Effort and cost are low at initiation, peak during execution and fall off at closure. The ability to influence the project's final cost is highest at the start and lowest at the end, while the cost of making changes rises steadily through the life cycle. This is why careful feasibility study and planning save money later.
The Planning Process

Typical planning steps
1. Define objectives (SMART) and the project scope
2. Break the scope into a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)
3. List activities for each work package
4. Establish logical dependencies (sequence)
5. Estimate duration, resources and cost of each activity
6. Prepare the schedule (bar chart / CPM / PERT network)
7. Allocate and level resources; prepare the budget
8. Plan quality, risk, communication and procurement
9. Approve the baseline plan and set up monitoring

A Work Breakdown Structure is a deliverable-oriented hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into smaller, manageable parts. Level 1 is the whole project; lower levels divide it into sub-projects, deliverables and finally work packages. A work package is the lowest level of the WBS, small enough to be estimated, scheduled, assigned to one responsible party and controlled. The 100 percent rule says the WBS must include all of the work, and only the work, in the scope.
Project objectives should be SMART:
items: Specific: clearly states what is to be achieved.
Measurable: progress and achievement can be quantified.
Achievable (attainable): realistic with available resources.
Relevant (realistic): aligned with the organisation's goals.
Time-bound: has a defined deadline.

concepts.text: The Triple Constraint

Scope, time and cost form the triple constraint (the iron triangle), with quality at its centre. Changing one side affects the others: adding scope needs more time or money, and cutting the schedule usually raises cost or reduces scope. Project success is judged by delivering the agreed scope at the required quality, on time and within budget.

formulas.plainText: Project scope = sum of all work packages (100% rule)

notes.text: Remember the sequence initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, closure. Monitoring and control overlaps execution rather than following it.
The work package, not the activity, is the lowest level of the WBS. Activities are then listed under each work package for scheduling.
Do not confuse a project with operations: repetitive, ongoing work such as maintenance of a running plant is operations, even if it is large.

formulas.title: Triple constraint
formulas.description: Scope, time and cost are interdependent; changing one affects the others and the achievable quality.

formulas.title: WBS 100% rule
formulas.plainText: Project scope = sum of all work packages
formulas.description: The work packages of a WBS together must cover all of the project scope and nothing outside it.

flashcards.front: What are the five phases (process groups) of a project life cycle?
flashcards.back: Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, and closure.
The lowest level of the WBS: a unit of work small enough to be estimated, scheduled, assigned to one responsible party and controlled.

flashcards.front: When in the life cycle is the ability to influence project cost highest?
flashcards.back: At the start (initiation and planning); the cost of making changes rises as the project progresses.

questions.questionText: Which sequence correctly orders the project life-cycle phases?
options: Planning, initiation, execution, closure, monitoring and control
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, closure
Initiation, execution, planning, closure, monitoring and control
Feasibility, closure, planning, execution, monitoring and control
questions.explanation: A project is first initiated (idea, feasibility, charter), then planned, executed with monitoring and control alongside, and finally closed.

questions.questionText: In a Work Breakdown Structure, the lowest level at which cost and duration are estimated and responsibility is assigned is called the:
questions.explanation: The work package is the lowest level of the WBS; it is small enough to estimate, schedule, assign and control.

questions.questionText: The 'triple constraint' of project management refers to:
questions.explanation: Scope, time and cost are the three interdependent constraints, with quality at the centre of the triangle.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the SMART criteria for project objectives?
questions.explanation: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound; 'standardised' is not part of it.

questions.questionText: A municipality runs routine annual maintenance of its existing street lights and, separately, builds a new 2 km drainage line with a fixed budget and deadline. Which statement is correct?
options: Both are projects because both use a budget
Both are operations because the municipality is the owner
The drainage line is a project; the routine maintenance is an operation
The maintenance is a project; the drainage line is an operation
questions.explanation: A project is temporary and produces a unique result; the new drainage line fits this, while repetitive ongoing maintenance is operations.

subtopics.title: Bar Charts & the Critical Path Method (CPM)
subtopics.subtitle: Gantt charts, AOA/AON networks, forward and backward pass, floats and crashing

concepts.text: Bar (Gantt) Charts and Milestone Charts

A bar chart, developed by Henry Gantt, lists activities on the vertical axis and shows each as a horizontal bar against a time scale; the bar length equals the activity duration. It is simple, easy to read and good for showing planned versus actual progress to site staff and clients. A milestone chart is a variation that marks key events (milestones), such as completion of foundation or commissioning, which have zero duration.
Limitations of bar charts that led to network methods:
items: Interdependencies between activities are not shown, so the effect of one delay on others cannot be seen.
The critical activities and the float of non-critical activities cannot be identified.
Not suitable for large, complex projects with hundreds of activities.
Uncertainty in durations cannot be represented, and updating after changes is laborious.

concepts.text: Network Diagrams: AOA and AON

A dummy activity in an AOA network is shown by a dashed arrow; it consumes no time and no resources. It is used to show a logical dependency that cannot otherwise be drawn and to give two parallel activities between the same events unique i-j numbers. Fulkerson's rule numbers the events: number the start event 1, delete its outgoing arrows, number the new initial events next, and repeat, so every arrow goes from a lower to a higher number.
Forward and Backward Pass

The forward pass starts at time 0 and computes the earliest start (ES) and earliest finish (EF) of each activity; where several activities merge, ES is the maximum of the predecessors' EF. The backward pass starts from the project duration at the end and computes latest finish (LF) and latest start (LS); where activities burst, LF is the minimum of the successors' LS.

concepts.latex: EF = ES + t,\quad LS = LF - t,\quad TF = LS - ES = LF - EF
concepts.plainText: EF = ES + t; LS = LF − t; Total float TF = LS − ES = LF − EF

concepts.text: Types of float (slack) of an activity i-j:
items: Total float: time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project; TF = LS − ES.
Free float: delay possible without delaying the earliest start of any successor; FF = ES(successor) − EF.
Independent float: delay possible without affecting predecessors or successors even when predecessors finish late and successors start early; IF = ES(j) − LF(i) − t, taken as zero if negative.
Always IF ≤ FF ≤ TF. Critical activities have zero total float.

concepts.text: Worked Network Example

Act  Pred  t | ES  EF | LS  LF | TF  FF
A    -     3 |  0   3 |  0   3 |  0   0
B    -     4 |  0   4 |  1   5 |  1   1
C    A     2 |  3   5 |  3   5 |  0   0
D    A     4 |  3   7 |  4   8 |  1   1
E    B,C   3 |  5   8 |  5   8 |  0   0
F    D,E   4 |  8  12 |  8  12 |  0   0
Project duration = 12; critical path A-C-E-F (3+2+3+4)

In the example, E cannot start until both B (EF 4) and C (EF 5) finish, so ES(E) = 5. Paths are A-D-F = 11, A-C-E-F = 12 and B-E-F = 11, so the longest path, and hence the critical path, is A-C-E-F with duration 12. B and D each have 1 day of total float.
Crashing and Time-Cost Trade-off

Crashing shortens the project by spending extra money (overtime, more crews, better equipment) on selected activities. Direct cost rises as duration is reduced, while indirect cost (overheads, supervision) falls; the optimum duration gives minimum total cost. Crash only critical activities, starting with the one having the lowest cost slope, and recheck the network after each step because new critical paths may appear.

concepts.plainText: Cost slope = (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time)

formulas.latex: EF = ES + t,\quad LS = LF - t
formulas.plainText: EF = ES + t; LS = LF − t

formulas.latex: TF = LS - ES = LF - EF,\quad FF = ES_{succ} - EF
formulas.plainText: TF = LS − ES = LF − EF; FF = ES(successor) − EF
Cost slope = (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time)

notes.text: The critical path is the longest path through the network; it fixes the shortest possible project duration. List all paths and add durations to check your forward pass.
At a merge take the MAXIMUM EF for ES in the forward pass; at a burst take the MINIMUM LS for LF in the backward pass. Mixing these up is the most common error.
Crashing a non-critical activity only adds cost without shortening the project. Crash the critical activity with the lowest cost slope first.

formulas.title: Forward and backward pass
formulas.latex: EF = ES + t,\quad LS = LF - t
formulas.plainText: EF = ES + t; LS = LF − t
formulas.description: Earliest finish adds the duration to earliest start; latest start subtracts it from latest finish.

formulas.title: Total float
formulas.description: Time an activity can slip without delaying project completion; zero on the critical path.

formulas.title: Free float
formulas.description: Delay an activity can absorb without delaying the earliest start of any successor.

formulas.title: Crash cost slope
formulas.plainText: Cost slope = (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time)
formulas.description: Extra direct cost per unit time saved; crash the critical activity with the lowest slope first.

flashcards.front: What is a dummy activity in an AOA network?
flashcards.back: A dashed arrow that takes no time or resources, used to show logical dependency or to give parallel activities unique event numbers.

flashcards.front: What is the main limitation of a bar (Gantt) chart?
flashcards.back: It does not show interdependencies between activities, so the critical activities and floats cannot be identified.

flashcards.front: State the relation between total, free and independent float.
flashcards.back: Independent float ≤ free float ≤ total float; all three are zero for critical activities.

flashcards.front: What is Fulkerson's rule used for?
flashcards.back: Numbering events in an AOA network so that every arrow goes from a lower-numbered to a higher-numbered event.

questions.questionText: A project has activities P (4 days, start), Q (6 days, after P), R (3 days, after P), S (5 days, after R) and T (2 days, after Q and S). What is the project duration and critical path?
questions.explanation: Path P-Q-T = 4+6+2 = 12 days and path P-R-S-T = 4+3+5+2 = 14 days; the longest path P-R-S-T is critical, giving 14 days.

questions.questionText: In the network P (4, start), Q (6, after P), R (3, after P), S (5, after R), T (2, after Q and S), what is the total float of activity Q?
questions.explanation: ES(Q) = 4, EF(Q) = 10; T starts at 12 (after S finishes at 12), so LF(Q) = 12 and TF = 12 − 10 = 2 days.

questions.questionText: In an activity-on-arrow network, a dummy activity:
options: Consumes neither time nor resources and shows only a logical dependency
Represents a critical activity with zero float
Represents a milestone with a fixed duration
questions.explanation: A dummy is drawn as a dashed arrow with zero duration and zero resources; it maintains correct logic and unique activity numbering.

questions.questionText: An activity has normal duration 10 days at Rs 50,000 and crash duration 7 days at Rs 62,000. Its cost slope is:
To reduce project duration at minimum extra cost, which activity should be crashed first?
options: The non-critical activity with the largest float
The longest activity in the project, whether critical or not
The critical activity with the highest cost slope
The critical activity with the lowest cost slope
questions.explanation: Only critical activities shorten the project, and choosing the one with the lowest cost slope gives the cheapest time saving.

subtopics.title: PERT: Three-Time Estimates & Probability of Completion
subtopics.subtitle: Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic times, beta distribution, variance and Z-value

concepts.text: Why PERT

PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) was developed in 1958 for the US Navy's Polaris missile programme, where many activities were new and their durations uncertain. Instead of a single duration, each activity is given three time estimates, and the method yields both the expected project duration and the probability of finishing by a given date. It is event-oriented and probabilistic, whereas CPM is activity-oriented and deterministic.
The three time estimates for each activity:
items: Optimistic time (a or t_o): shortest time if everything goes exceptionally well.
Most likely time (m or t_m): the time needed under normal conditions; the mode of the distribution.
Pessimistic time (b or t_p): longest time if things go badly, excluding major catastrophes.

concepts.text: Beta Distribution, Expected Time and Variance

Activity duration is assumed to follow a beta distribution, which is bounded between a and b and can be skewed either way. From this assumption the expected (mean) time is a weighted average giving the most likely time four times the weight of the extremes, and the standard deviation is one-sixth of the range.
Path Variance and Probability of Completion

The expected project duration T_e is the sum of t_e along the critical path. By the central limit theorem, the project duration is taken as normally distributed, with variance equal to the SUM of the variances of the critical activities. Standard deviations are not added directly; take the square root of the summed variance.

Critical path: A then B
Act   a   m   b |  t_e  sigma  variance
A     4  10  28 |  12     4      16
B     5  11  23 |  12     3       9
T_e = 12 + 12 = 24 weeks; variance = 25; sigma_path = 5
P(finish within T_s = 29 weeks):
Z = (29 - 24)/5 = 1.0 -> P = 0.8413 = 84.1%
P(finish within 24 weeks): Z = 0 -> 50%
Useful standard normal values (area to the left of Z):
items: Z = 0 gives 50%: a schedule equal to the expected time has only an even chance.
Z = 1.0 gives about 84.1%; Z = 1.5 about 93.3%; Z = 2.0 about 97.7%; Z = 3.0 about 99.9%.
Negative Z gives probabilities below 50%, e.g. Z = −1.0 gives about 15.9%.

concepts.text: CPM versus PERT

rows: Repetitive work with known durations, e.g. construction
New, R&D-type projects with uncertain durations

notes.text: Add VARIANCES along the critical path, not standard deviations. Two activities with σ = 3 and σ = 4 give σ_path = 5, not 7.
If the scheduled time equals the expected time, the probability of completion is exactly 50 percent; it is a quick check on any PERT answer.
Individual activity times follow a beta distribution, but the project duration (sum of many activities) is treated as normal by the central limit theorem.

formulas.title: PERT expected time
formulas.description: Weighted mean of optimistic, most likely (weight 4) and pessimistic times from the beta distribution.

formulas.title: Activity standard deviation
formulas.description: One-sixth of the range between pessimistic and optimistic times; its square is the variance.

formulas.title: Probability of completion
formulas.description: Standard normal value for a scheduled time T_s; read the probability from the normal table.

flashcards.front: Which probability distribution does PERT assume for activity durations?
flashcards.back: The beta distribution; the overall project duration is then treated as normally distributed.

flashcards.front: What is the probability of completing a project by its expected duration T_e?
flashcards.back: 50 percent, because Z = 0 at T_s = T_e.

flashcards.front: How is the standard deviation of the critical path found?
flashcards.back: Add the variances of the critical activities and take the square root of the sum.

questions.questionText: An activity has optimistic time 4 days, most likely time 6 days and pessimistic time 14 days. Its PERT expected time is:
For an activity with optimistic time 2 weeks and pessimistic time 14 weeks, the variance of its duration is:
questions.explanation: σ = (14 − 2)/6 = 2 weeks, so variance σ² = 4 weeks².

questions.questionText: A project's expected duration along the critical path is 40 weeks with a path standard deviation of 4 weeks. The probability of completing it within 46 weeks is about:
questions.explanation: Z = (46 − 40)/4 = 1.5, and the area to the left of Z = 1.5 is about 0.933, i.e. 93.3%.

questions.questionText: The critical path of a PERT network has two activities with standard deviations of 3 days and 4 days. The standard deviation of the project duration is:
questions.explanation: Variances add: 9 + 16 = 25, so σ_path = √25 = 5 days; standard deviations are not added directly.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes PERT from CPM?
options: PERT is probabilistic and event-oriented; CPM is deterministic and activity-oriented
PERT uses one time estimate; CPM uses three time estimates
PERT is mainly used for crashing; CPM is used for probability of completion
PERT cannot identify a critical path; CPM can
questions.explanation: PERT uses three time estimates and gives probabilities (event-oriented), while CPM uses single deterministic durations and supports time-cost trade-off.

subtopics.title: Resource Levelling & Resource Smoothing
subtopics.subtitle: Resource histograms, loading, levelling vs smoothing, using float and allocation

concepts.text: Resources in Scheduling

A CPM or PERT schedule assumes unlimited resources, but labour, equipment, materials and money are always limited in practice. If every activity starts at its earliest start, demand for a resource usually shows sharp peaks and valleys, causing idle crews on some days and shortages on others. Resource management adjusts the timing of activities so that demand is practical and economical.
Key terms:
items: Resource loading (aggregation): adding up, period by period, the resource requirement of all activities in a given schedule.
Resource histogram: bar chart of resource units required against time; the ideal shape is roughly rectangular (uniform).
Resource allocation: assigning available resources to activities, deciding priorities when demand exceeds supply.
Resource-days (man-days): resource units × duration; the total area under the histogram.

concepts.plainText: Average resource demand = Σ(resource rate × duration) / project duration T

concepts.text: Levelling versus Smoothing

rows: Any activity, including critical ones if needed
Reduce peaks and valleys in demand
Keep demand within the available limit

concepts.text: Terminology differs between books: some Indian texts use 'levelling' for the time-constrained case, while PMBOK uses levelling for the resource-constrained case in which the finish date may slip and smoothing when it may not. MCQs often turn on the key difference: smoothing never changes the project end date, whereas levelling can.
Using Float to Smooth Demand

Project duration 6 days (A is critical); B, C, D independent
Act  Dur  Workers  ES  TF
A     6     3       0   0
B     2     3       0   4
C     2     3       0   4
D     2     3       0   4
Early start:  days 1-2 = 3+3+3+3 = 12, days 3-6 = 3  (peak 12)
Shift C to days 3-4 and D to days 5-6 (within float)
Smoothed:     every day = 6 workers  (peak 6, duration still 6)

Total demand is 3×6 + 3×(3×2) = 36 worker-days in both schedules, so the average is 36/6 = 6 workers. Shifting non-critical activities within their float moved the peak from 12 down to the average without changing the finish date. The area under the histogram is unchanged by smoothing; only its shape changes.
Heuristics and Priority Rules
Practical rules used in levelling and allocation (e.g. Burgess method, serial scheduling):
items: Schedule critical activities first; move activities with the largest float before those with little float.
When resources conflict, give priority to the activity with the least total float or the earliest late start.
Burgess method: try alternative start times and choose the schedule with the minimum sum of squares of daily resource demand.
Recompute floats after each shift, because moving one activity can use up float of its successors.

concepts.plainText: Burgess method: minimise the sum over days of (daily resource demand)²

formulas.plainText: Average resource demand = Σ(r_i × t_i) / T

notes.text: Smoothing = project end date fixed, move only within float. Levelling = resource limit fixed, project may take longer.
Shifting activities never changes the total resource-days (area of the histogram); it only redistributes demand over time.
Moving a non-critical activity beyond its total float delays the whole project; moving it beyond its free float delays its successors.

formulas.title: Average resource demand
formulas.plainText: Average resource demand = Σ(r_i × t_i) / T
formulas.description: Total resource-days divided by project duration; the target level of a well-smoothed histogram.

formulas.title: Burgess levelling criterion
formulas.plainText: Minimise Σ R_d² over all days
formulas.description: The schedule with the smallest sum of squared daily demands has the most uniform resource histogram.

flashcards.front: Does resource smoothing change the project duration?
flashcards.back: No. Smoothing moves only non-critical activities within their float, so the finish date stays fixed.
A bar chart showing the units of a resource required in each time period; ideally it is nearly uniform.

flashcards.front: Why may resource levelling extend a project?
flashcards.back: Because demand must be kept within a fixed resource limit, even critical activities may have to be delayed.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes resource smoothing?
options: Delaying critical activities to stay within a resource limit
Rescheduling non-critical activities within their float without changing project duration
Crashing activities to reduce project duration
Adding resources to all activities to finish early
questions.explanation: Smoothing is time-constrained: it reduces peaks and valleys by using float, keeping the project end date unchanged.

questions.questionText: A 6-day project has P (days 1-4, 3 workers), Q (days 1-2, 4 workers, total float 4 days) and R (days 3-6, 2 workers). If Q is shifted to days 5-6, the peak daily requirement becomes:
questions.explanation: After shifting: days 1-2 = 3, days 3-4 = 3 + 2 = 5, days 5-6 = 2 + 4 = 6, so the peak falls from 7 to 6 workers.

questions.questionText: When resource availability is strictly limited and cannot be exceeded, resource levelling may result in:
options: No effect on any activity start times
An extension of the project duration
questions.explanation: Resource-constrained levelling may delay even critical activities to keep demand within the limit, so the project can take longer.

questions.questionText: In the Burgess method of resource levelling, the preferred schedule is the one that minimises:
options: The sum of squares of daily resource requirements
The total float of all activities
The number of activities on the critical path
The total resource-days of the project
questions.explanation: Since total resource-days are fixed, minimising the sum of squared daily demands produces the most uniform histogram.

questions.questionText: While smoothing resources, which activities should normally be rescheduled first?
options: Activities with the longest duration regardless of float
Non-critical activities with the largest float
questions.explanation: Activities with the most float can be moved furthest without delaying the project, so they are shifted first.

subtopics.title: Project Monitoring, Evaluation & Control
subtopics.subtitle: Monitoring vs evaluation, control cycle, S-curves, earned value and the logical framework

concepts.text: Monitoring, Evaluation and Control

Monitoring is the continuous, routine collection and analysis of information on progress, cost and quality during implementation, comparing actual performance with the plan. Evaluation is a periodic, systematic assessment of a project's relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability. Control is the action taken when monitoring shows a deviation: correcting the work, revising the plan or changing resources.

rows: Are we doing things right, as planned?
Are we doing the right things; did it work?

concepts.text: Types of evaluation by timing and purpose:
items: Ex-ante (appraisal): before implementation, to judge feasibility.
Formative (on-going or mid-term): during implementation, to improve the project while it runs.
Summative (terminal): at completion, to judge overall achievement of objectives.
Ex-post (impact): some years after completion, to assess long-term impact and sustainability.

concepts.text: The Control Cycle and Progress Reporting

Control cycle
1. Set the baseline (scope, schedule, budget, quality standards)
2. Measure actual performance (site records, timesheets, invoices)
3. Compare actual with planned; compute variances
4. Analyse causes of deviation and forecast the outcome
5. Take corrective action; update the plan
6. Report and repeat each reporting period

Progress is reported through periodic reports, updated bar charts and networks, milestone reports and cost reports. An S-curve plots cumulative cost or work against time; it is S-shaped because progress is slow at the start, fast in the middle and slow again near completion. Plotting the actual and earned curves against the planned S-curve shows at a glance whether the project is ahead or behind and over or under budget.
Earned Value Management
Earned value management (EVM) integrates scope, schedule and cost using three values at the status date:
items: Planned Value (PV, or BCWS): budgeted cost of the work scheduled to date.
Earned Value (EV, or BCWP): budgeted cost of the work actually performed; EV = percent complete × BAC.
Actual Cost (AC, or ACWP): actual cost incurred for the work performed.
Budget at Completion (BAC): the total approved budget.

concepts.latex: CV = EV - AC,\quad SV = EV - PV
concepts.plainText: Cost variance CV = EV − AC; Schedule variance SV = EV − PV
CPI = EV/AC; SPI = EV/PV; EAC = BAC/CPI

concepts.text:
BAC = Rs 100 lakh; at month 5: PV = 50, EV = 40, AC = 45 (Rs lakh)
CV  = 40 - 45 = -5    (over budget)
SV  = 40 - 50 = -10   (behind schedule)
CPI = 40/45 = 0.889   SPI = 40/50 = 0.80
EAC = 100/0.889 = 112.5 lakh
ETC = EAC - AC = 112.5 - 45 = 67.5 lakh
VAC = BAC - EAC = 100 - 112.5 = -12.5 lakh

Negative variances and indices below 1 are unfavourable: CPI < 1 means over budget and SPI < 1 means behind schedule. EAC = BAC/CPI assumes the current cost efficiency continues to completion; other forecasts exist, such as EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) when the overrun is expected to be a one-off.
Logical Framework (Logframe)

The logical framework is a 4 × 4 matrix widely used by governments and donors for planning, monitoring and evaluation. Its rows form the vertical logic from goal to purpose (outcome) to outputs to activities (with inputs). Its columns are the narrative summary, objectively verifiable indicators (OVIs), means of verification (MOVs) and important assumptions or risks.

formulas.latex: CV = EV - AC,\quad SV = EV - PV
formulas.plainText: CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV

formulas.latex: EAC = \dfrac{BAC}{CPI},\quad ETC = EAC - AC,\quad VAC = BAC - EAC
formulas.plainText: EAC = BAC/CPI; ETC = EAC − AC; VAC = BAC − EAC

notes.text: Every EVM formula starts with EV: CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV. Negative or below 1 means bad news.
Comparing actual cost with planned value alone (AC vs PV) is misleading; without EV you cannot tell whether spending reflects progress or overrun.
Monitoring is continuous and internal; evaluation is periodic and often independent. Formative evaluation improves a running project, summative judges it at the end.

formulas.title: Cost and schedule variance
formulas.latex: CV = EV - AC,\quad SV = EV - PV
formulas.plainText: CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV
formulas.description: Negative CV means over budget; negative SV means less work done than planned.

formulas.title: Performance indices
formulas.description: Values below 1 show cost overrun (CPI) or schedule delay (SPI).

formulas.title: Estimate at completion
formulas.description: Forecast of total cost assuming the current cost efficiency continues to the end.

formulas.title: Earned value
formulas.description: Budgeted value of the work actually performed to the status date.

flashcards.back: Monitoring is continuous tracking of progress against plan during implementation; evaluation is a periodic assessment of outcomes, impact and sustainability.
Only 80 percent of the work planned to date has been done, so the project is behind schedule.

flashcards.front: What are the four columns of a logframe matrix?
flashcards.back: Narrative summary, objectively verifiable indicators, means of verification, and important assumptions.

flashcards.front: Why is a project's cumulative cost curve S-shaped?
flashcards.back: Spending is slow during mobilisation, rapid during peak execution and slows again near completion.

questions.questionText: A project has BAC = Rs 80 lakh and is 30% complete; the actual cost so far is Rs 30 lakh. Its cost performance index (CPI) is:
questions.explanation: EV = 0.30 × 80 = Rs 24 lakh, so CPI = EV/AC = 24/30 = 0.80, indicating a cost overrun.

questions.questionText: At a status date the planned value is Rs 60 lakh and the earned value is Rs 48 lakh. The schedule performance index and status are:
questions.explanation: SPI = EV/PV = 48/60 = 0.80; a value below 1 means less work has been done than planned.

questions.questionText: A project with budget at completion Rs 200 lakh is running at CPI = 0.8. If this efficiency continues, the estimate at completion (EAC) is:
questions.explanation: EAC = BAC/CPI = 200/0.8 = Rs 250 lakh.

questions.questionText: An evaluation carried out midway through implementation, mainly to improve the project while it is still running, is called:
questions.explanation: Formative (on-going or mid-term) evaluation is done during implementation to guide improvements; summative is at the end and ex-post is years later.

questions.questionText: The columns of a logical framework (logframe) matrix are:
options: Planned value, earned value, actual cost and budget
Narrative summary, objectively verifiable indicators, means of verification and assumptions
questions.explanation: Goal, purpose, outputs and activities are the rows (vertical logic); the columns are narrative summary, OVIs, MOVs and important assumptions.
